target: Hannah Saniger, born about 1805–1815, married James Wakefield, and had her first children baptised — somewhere — in Bristol

anglican.test: William and Mary SMITH, across Gloucestershire, for the twenty-one years 1800–1820.
anglican.verdict: Two hundred and eighty-nine entries, seventy-five parishes, and ONE of them inside Bristol — Stapleton, on the edge of the city, with a single entry. Not one Bristol city parish appears at all.
anglican.so: FreeREG has essentially no Bristol for 1800–1820. Every search this archive has run for a Bristol baptism has been searching a city that is not in the index, and the emptiness it kept returning was the index's, not the family's.

access: All twelve were checked one by one against The National Archives' own record details. Every one comes back DIGITISED: FALSE. RG 4 is filmed and published through commercial partners, not free on TNA's website — so these cannot be read from a desk without a subscription, and this archive said the opposite this morning.

swept.head: Answered — and not by reading twelve volumes
swept.lede: The errand assumed these registers would have to be read one at a time, because RG 4 is filmed through commercial partners and not free on The National Archives' site. **It did not come to that.** FindMyPast carries the RG 4 transcriptions as **England & Wales Non-Conformist Births and Baptisms** and **England & Wales Non-Conformist Burials**, and both are searchable by place.
swept.body:
**The surname box takes wildcards, so the whole question fits in one query.** `S*N*G*R` at **Bristol** in the baptism set returns **nought** — no Saniger, Sanigar, Sinegar, Sinnegar, Sainger, Sanigor or any other form, in any Bristol chapel, in the whole series.

**Three controls, same session, same query shape.** SMITH at Bristol in that set returns **133** chapel baptisms, Congregational and Presbyterian, between 1724 and 1831 — so the Bristol chapels are indexed. The same wildcard with no place returns **808** — so the wildcard works. And SANIGAR returns **8** — so the surname is in the set. The chapels are there, the name is there, and they do not meet.

**The burials say the same thing more usefully still.** `S*N*G*R` at Bristol in the burial set returns **nine rows and not one of them is this name**: Singer five times, Springer, Stringer twice, Swearenger, Baptist and Presbyterian, 1704 to 1812. A null that returns nine near misses at the right place is about as controlled as a null gets.
swept.denomHead: But the family was chapel — thirty miles up the scarp
swept.denom:
The eight SANIGAR entries are all at **one chapel: Dursley, Corn Meeting, Congregational.** Rose, daughter of Willm, in **1781**; then **Thomas Browning Sanigar's** children — Emily Sophia 1851, Fanny 1852, Rachel Harris 1854, Edward Thomas 1856 — and **Thomas Sanigar's** — Susanna 1861, Albert Thomas 1863, Hester Jane 1866.

So this page's closing caveat has to be rewritten. It said **nothing yet suggests the Sanigers were nonconformist**, and that is no longer true: the **scarp branch was Congregational for at least eighty years**. What remains true, and is the point, is that **it was Congregational at Dursley and not at Bristol.** The hypothesis this page was built on has been tested where it mattered and it failed there.
swept.ingestHead: And a fact about the other set, which changes a number
swept.ingest: Those same eight entries also appear in **England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975** — Rose 1781, Fanny 1852, Rachel Harris 1854, Susanna 1860 and the rest. **That set is not purely Anglican**: it ingests RG 4 too. Some of the duplication measured on [/spellings](/spellings/) is therefore not a register typed up twice but **one register reaching the index by two routes**, which is a better explanation than the one that page offers and is now recorded on both.
